{{Other uses|Collapse (disambiguation){{!}}Collapse}}

In [[topology]], a branch of mathematics, a '''collapse''' reduces a [[simplicial complex]] (or more generally, a [[CW complex]]) to a [[Homotopy#Homotopy_equivalence|homotopy-equivalent]] subcomplex. Collapses, like CW complexes themselves, were invented by [[J. H. C. Whitehead]].<ref name="Whitehead">{{cite journal|authorlink=J. H. C. Whitehead|last=Whitehead|first= J.H.C.| year=1938|title=Simplicial spaces, nuclei and ''m''-groups|journal= [[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]]|volume= 45|pages=243–327}}</ref> Collapses find applications in [[Computational topology#Computational homology|computational homology]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Computational homology|first=Tomasz|last=Kaczynski|date=2004|publisher=Springer|others=Mischaikow, Konstantin Michael, Mrozek, Marian|isbn=9780387215976|location=New York|oclc=55897585}}</ref>

==Definition==

Let <math>K</math> be an  [[abstract simplicial complex]].

Suppose that <math>\tau, \sigma</math> are two simplices of <math>K</math> such that the following two conditions are satisfied: 
# <math>\tau \subsetneq \sigma,</math> in particular <math>\dim \tau < \dim \sigma;</math>
# <math>\sigma</math> is a maximal face of <math>K</math> and no other maximal face of <math>K</math> contains <math>\tau,</math>

then <math>\tau</math> is called a '''free face'''. 

A simplicial '''collapse''' of <math>K</math> is the removal of all simplices <math>\gamma</math> such that <math>\tau \subseteq \gamma \subseteq \sigma,</math> where <math>\tau</math> is a free face. If additionally we have <math>\dim \tau = \dim \sigma - 1,</math> then this is called an '''elementary collapse'''. 

A simplicial complex that has a sequence of collapses leading to a point is called '''collapsible'''. Every collapsible complex is [[Contractible space|contractible]], but the converse is not true.

This definition can be extended to [[CW-complex]]es and is the basis for the concept of [[simple-homotopy equivalence]].<ref>Cohen, Marshall M. (1973) ''A Course in Simple-Homotopy Theory'', Springer-Verlag New York</ref>

==Examples==

* Complexes that do not have a free face cannot be collapsible.  Two such interesting examples are [[R. H. Bing]]'s [[house with two rooms]] and [[Christopher Zeeman]]'s [[Dunce hat (topology)|dunce hat]]; they are [[contractible]] (homotopy equivalent to a point), but not collapsible.
* Any ''n''-dimensional [[PL manifold]] that is collapsible is in fact piecewise-linearly isomorphic to an ''n''-ball.<ref name="Whitehead" />
